title: How Sites Store Passwords
objective: After this level you can explain why a well-run site keeps only a scrambled hash of your password, never the password itself.
summary: A good site stores a salted, deliberately slow hash of your password: a one-way jumble it can check at login but cannot turn back into the password.

cards.headline: A good website doesn't know your password.
cards.body: Yet it can tell, every time, whether you typed the right one. It sounds like a magic trick. It's really a smart way of checking a secret without keeping it, and it matters most on the day a site gets robbed.

cards.headline: The blender
cards.body: A hash function takes input of any length, a word or a whole book, and turns out a jumble of fixed length. It works one way only: working back from the jumble to the input is computationally infeasible. Think of a blender. Strawberries go in, a smoothie comes out, and nobody is getting the strawberries back.

cards.headline: Checking without knowing
cards.body: So a well-run site stores only the hash of your password. When you log in, it hashes whatever you just typed and compares the two jumbles. Match, and the door opens. A thief who copies the site's password list gets smoothies, not passwords.

cards.headline: Hashing is not encryption
cards.body: Encryption is two-way: with the key, scrambled text turns back into the original. Hashing is one-way: there's no key and nothing to decrypt. For passwords, that's the whole point. If a site encrypted your password instead, anyone who got hold of the key could read it.

mascot.line: People mix these two up all the time. Encryption locks and unlocks with a key. A hash never unlocks at all.

cards.headline: A pinch of salt, and a slow blender
cards.body: Identical passwords would give identical hashes, and attackers keep ready-made tables of hashes for common passwords. So sites add a salt: a unique random value mixed into each password before hashing. Now identical passwords get different hashes and the tables are useless. Good sites also choose a deliberately slow hash, because a fast one lets a thief test guesses at great speed. NIST, the US standards agency, requires passwords to be stored salted and hashed.

cards.headline: Passwords: blended
learned: A hash turns any input into a fixed-length, one-way jumble
Sites hash what you type and compare it with the stored hash
Hashing is one-way; encryption can be undone with a key
Salts and slow hashes make stolen hashes hard to crack

questions.prompt: What does a well-run website keep so it can check your password at login?

options.label: Your password, written in a locked file
options.rationale: Keeping the password itself is exactly what good sites avoid.

options.label: Only a hash of your password
The first three letters of your password
options.rationale: It stores a hash of the whole password.

options.label: Nothing; it asks your email provider each time
options.rationale: The site checks against the hash it stores.

questions.explanation: The site stores only the hash; at login it hashes what you type and compares the two.

questions.prompt: Match each password-safety idea with its description.
questions.explanation: Encryption is two-way, hashing is one-way, and a salt is a unique random value mixed into each password before hashing.

questions.prompt: Level 51 said all systems contain vulnerabilities. Why does a site storing only hashes still matter if it is well built?

options.label: Because hashes stop every attack on the site from ever happening
options.rationale: Hashing limits the damage; it does not prevent every break-in.

options.label: Because if a flaw lets a thief copy the list, they get hashes, not passwords
Because hashing patches the site's software flaws automatically
options.rationale: Patches fix flaws; hashing protects the stored passwords.

options.label: Because well-built sites never have flaws
options.rationale: All systems contain vulnerabilities, even good ones.

questions.explanation: Since every system can have holes, sites plan for a break-in: a stolen list of hashes does not reveal the passwords.
